description: Our team represents college from Chernivtsy National University
summary:
Our challenge was to create a game where children can explore and do exciting things on Mars. We built Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer: a 3D browser game where kids walk around a space base and decide how to use limited solar energy each work shift – keep the crew alive with Life Support, or run the Science Lab.

The main idea is consequences. If a child picks one option instead of another, the crew can (figuratively) die. Our first mission takes place near the Moon's south pole: halfway through, the Sun hides behind a ridge, real shadows cover the solar panels and power drops to zero, so players must save energy in advance. The lighting is based on NASA imagery of the lunar south pole. The next mission brings the same choices to Mars, where a dust storm blocks the sunlight.

The game is simple on purpose. We believe children will remember how they walked on another world and made choices – and that real astronauts will face the same choices one day. We plan to keep developing the project.

details:
What it does and how it works

Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a 3D browser game in which a child becomes a young astronaut at a space base. The player walks freely around the base in first person and explores the modules, the solar panels, rover tracks and the Earth in the sky.

The mission is divided into work shifts. Before each shift, the child decides where to send the solar energy: to Life Support, to keep the crew safe, or to the Science Lab, to study samples. There is never enough energy for everything at once. Whatever is not used is stored in a battery for later.

The first mission, "The Long Shadow", takes place near the Moon's south pole. Halfway through, the Sun hides behind a ridge, a real shadow covers the solar panels, and they stop producing power. Players who did not save energy in advance risk leaving the crew without air. The next mission brings the same decisions to Mars, where a dust storm blocks the sunlight.

After every shift, the game explains in simple words what happened and why, so the child can see the link between their choice and its consequences.

Benefits

- Teaches children to think about consequences. Every decision changes something: if you choose one option instead of another, the crew can (figuratively) die. It is a safe way to feel that choices have a cost.

- Teaches planning ahead. At the start of the mission the game warns that a shadow is coming, so children learn not to spend everything at once and to save for the hard moment.

- Teaches priorities. People's safety comes first, science second – the same principle real space missions follow.

- Explains science without a textbook. Children see with their own eyes that the Sun on the Moon moves low, shadows are long, and solar power is not constant. It is not a number in a table, but something they experience in the game.

- Accessible to everyone. The game runs in an ordinary browser with no installation and makes no network requests once loaded, so it can be played at home or at school.

Intended impact

We want children to take away not only knowledge about space, but also the habit of thinking before acting. Resources are limited not only on the Moon or Mars, but in everyday life too: time, money, energy. We believe children will remember walking on another world and making important decisions – and that one day real astronauts will have to make the very same choices. Perhaps one of these children will become such an astronaut.

Tools and technologies

- JavaScript, HTML, CSS

- Three.js – a library for 3D graphics in the browser

- Vite – a tool for building and running the project

- Python and Playwright – automated tests that play through the game and check that everything works

- Git and GitHub – team collaboration on the code

- AI assistants (Claude, OpenAI Codex) – help with writing and testing the code

How the project is creative

- The shadow is real, not painted. In every shift the Sun is in a different position, and the shadow of the ridge physically covers the panels. A separate script casts rays from 60 points on the panels toward the Sun and checks that the lighting matches the amount of energy in the game.

- Everything is created with code. The terrain, rocks, base, Earth and starry sky are generated procedurally, without a single downloaded image, so the game is light and fast.

- Science at its core. The low Sun and long shadows are based on NASA imagery of the lunar south pole. Where we deliberately simplified things for children (the Sun is a bit higher, the Earth a bit larger), we documented it.

Factors we considered

- Simplicity. The game is simple on purpose, so children do not get lost in the rules and can focus on their choices.

- Fair consequences. Losing is not a punishment but an explanation: the game shows what went wrong and offers to try again.

- Accessibility. The game is controlled with the keyboard and mouse, has labels for screen readers, and adapts to slower computers.

- Future development. We plan to keep developing the project: a full Mars map, new missions and more base modules.
